# Generated files and how to regenerate them

Everything under `FourColor/` is either hand-written or generated by a script
in this directory; every generated module is kernel-checked like any other, so
nothing here is trusted by the proof.

## The reducibility certificates (self-contained)

`FourColor/Bulk/Cfg/*.lean`, `FourColor/Mask/*.lean` and
`FourColor/Reduce/All.lean` are produced from `FourColor/Configurations.lean`
alone:

```shell
scripts/gen_certificates.sh [workdir] [jobs]     # about one core-hour
```

which compiles and runs, in order,

| step | tool | output |
|---|---|---|
| colourings and contract colourings of each configuration | `tools/cpc.py` | `<workdir>/gen/<i>.in` |
| the bulk certificate (one-chord rule): rank, witness and choice planes, and the residual contract colourings | `tools/planes.c` | `<workdir>/planes/<i>.planes.gz` |
| the residual certificate of the configurations the bulk rule leaves: ranked witnesses and the entries each chord settles | `tools/residual.c` | `<workdir>/hybc/<i>.txt` |
| the Lean modules | `gen_groups.py`, `gen_bulk_jobs.py`, `gen_maskc_jobs.py`, `gen_hybt_jobs.py`, `gen_all.py` (helpers `bulkspace.py`, `certdata.py`) | the modules above |

The output is deterministic and reproduces the shipped modules byte for byte.

## Translations of the reference

`FourColor/Configurations.lean` (the 633 configurations) and
`FourColor/Present<n>*.lean` (the seven presentation scripts) were translated
mechanically, once, from `configurations.v` and `present<n>.v` of the reference
development ([rocq-community/fourcolor](https://github.com/rocq-community/fourcolor),
CeCILL-B; none of its text is copied into this repository), and the results are
committed.  `FourColor/QuizData.lean` and `QuizTreeData.lean` were then derived
from `Configurations.lean` by a Lean computation.  The translators are not kept
here: nothing in the proof trusts their output, which is data that the kernel
computations either accept or reject on its merits.

## Verification and measurement

* `check.sh` — builds everything, then runs `Check.lean` (the theorem's axioms;
  no `sorry`, no `native_decide`, no scratch modules) and `Audit.lean` (the
  negative controls).
* `build_pool.py` — the same `lean` invocations Lake would run, but never more
  than `--jobs` at a time and never admitting a module whose predicted peak
  would push the total past `--memory` (defaults: `min(32, 90% of cores)` and
  75 % of available memory).  This is what `build.sh` uses.

  Ready modules start in order of *critical path* — a module's own time plus
  the longest chain of modules waiting on it — so the long poles start early,
  and a module that does not fit the remaining budget is skipped over rather
  than waited for.  Both come from `module_cost.tsv` below.  `--dry-run`
  prints the plan and predicted makespan without building, which is how to
  sweep `--jobs` for the point where the build turns memory-bandwidth-bound.

* `module_cost.tsv` — per-module wall time and peak memory, committed so that a
  first build schedules well on an unfamiliar machine.  Peak memory carries
  across machines; times do not, but only their *ratios* matter to the
  ordering.  Every run writes its own measurements to
  `.lake/build/module_cost.tsv`, which overlays the committed table on the next
  run; `--save-profile scripts/module_cost.tsv` updates the committed one.

  It is only ever a hint.  The dependency graph is parsed afresh from the
  sources on every run, so a missing, stale or wrong table costs packing
  quality and nothing else — the build is the same build, and says so in a
  warning.
